Under the old-family membership stated in §2, the relevant adjacency table is:Vertex in  $A$ Neighbors in  $V$  $(1,a+6)$  $(1,a+5),(1,a+7),(2,a+6)$  $(2,a+5)$  $(1,a+5),(2,a+6),(3,a+5)$  $(2,a+7)$  $(1,a+7),(2,a+6),(3,a+7)$  $(3,a+6)$  $(2,a+6),(3,a+5),(3,a+7)$  $(3,a+8)$  $(3,a+7)$ Thus its union is exactly the displayed  $N$ . are the two indicated free vertices.There is an exact edge-counting identity behind the proposed inequality:
$$\sum_{w\in N}p_w-\sum_{w\in A}p_w
=
\sum_{\substack{\{z,w\}\in E(V)\\z\in N,\ w\notin A}}x_{\{z,w\}}
\ge 0.
\tag{H}$$
To see this, every edge incident to  $A$  joins  $A$  to  $N$ , and therefore contributes once to each of the two vertex sums. All remaining contributions to the  $N$ -sum are nonnegative. Since  $A$  and  $N$  each lie in a single parity class, there is no internal-edge multiplicity to account for.Four vertices on each side have prescribed endpoint weight  $1$ . Cancelling them in (H) gives exactly
$$p_{(2,6m+5)}\le p_{(3,6m+5)}.$$
For the preceding point,
$$p(A)=4+1=\frac{460}{92},\qquad
p(N)=4+\frac{61}{92}=\frac{429}{92}.$$
The deficit is therefore precisely
$$\frac{31}{92}.$$
This obstruction applies directly to fractional edge weights. No integrality theorem is needed, and allowing simultaneous fractional matching edges cannot evade it.The new seed is consistent with this obstruction: Appendix A gives
$$p_{(2,53)}=p_{(3,53)}=1.$$
It satisfies the terminal inequality at equality. Identity (H) then also requires zero matching weight from  $N$  to  $V\setminus A$ , which is consistent with the listed terminal edges.2. There is no extrapolation from finitely many tested lengths in the written argument.The essential convention is that, after expanding  $p$  and  $o$ , the horizontal support of a constraint includes both endpoint columns of every edge variable occurring in it. With this convention, take the asserted maximum support diameter to be  $6$ .Let
$$d=6(m-8).$$
The enlarged collar really is periodicFor  $d>0$ , the spliced assignment is periodic throughout
$$[20,40+d].$$

Also, when  $d>0$ , necessarily  $d\ge6$ , so the translated seed does not begin before column  $30$ .Thus the phrase “unchanged corresponding seed constraint” is correct.Right case. If  $S$  contains a column at least  $41+d$ , then

$$S\subseteq[20,40+d],$$
so the constraint is checked entirely by the periodic assignment.A support cannot meet both nonperiodic sides: the distance between a column at most  $19$  and one at least  $41+d$  exceeds  $6$ .For  $d=0$ , the construction recovers the seed. The splice increments and whole-board accounting are correctThere is no missing seam contribution or duplicated matching allowance.For an especially explicit edge count, put  $q=m-8\ge1$ , and work in units of  $1/80$ . The only positive edge crossing the original cut between columns  $23$  and  $24$  has weight  $24$ .The inserted block of  $q$  periods has internal edge weight
$$480q-24.$$
Its two exterior seam edges contribute  $24+24$ . Removing the original crossing contribution therefore gives
$$\Delta\!\left(\sum 80x\right)
=(480q-24)+24+24-24
=480q.$$
Thus
$$\sum_e x_e=\frac{4240+480(m-8)}{80}=6m+5.$$
Similarly,
$$\sum_{v\in U}t_v
=\frac{4786+614(m-8)}{80}
=\frac{614m-126}{80}.$$
Therefore
$$\begin{aligned}
J_m
&=(5m+14)+(6m+5)+\frac{614m-126}{80}\\
&=\frac{1494m+1394}{80}
=\frac{747m+697}{40}.
\end{aligned}$$
The whole-board nature of this calculation can also be seen from the general identity
$$2\sum_e x_e
=
|P_0|+\sum_{v\in U}p_v.$$
It implies
$$J
=
|R|+\frac{|P_0|}{2}
+\frac12\sum_{v\in U}(2t_v+p_v).
\tag{W}$$
For this construction, the contribution outside  $C_m$  is exactly  $63/80$ . Substituting into (W) gives
$$J_m
=
(5m+14)+\frac{8m+10}{2}
+\frac{1548m-315+63}{160},$$
which again yields the stated formula.Thus the pocket contribution and old endpoints are included; this is not merely a connected-band calculation presented as a whole-board result.The threshold arithmetic is also correct:
$$J_m-(18m+29)=\frac{27m-463}{40}.$$
Its first positive value for integral  $m$  is at  $m=18$ , where it equals  $23/40$ . In particular,
$$J_{18}=\frac{14143}{40}=353+\frac{23}{40}.$$
Likewise,
$$J_m-(18m+30)=\frac{27m-503}{40}>0
\qquad(m\ge19).$$
These are fractional violations. They do not establish an integer violation.5. The conclusion about matching-polytope integrality has the right scopeLet
$$P_G=\left\{x\ge0:\sum_{e\ni v}x_e\le1\text{ for every }v\right\}.$$
For a bipartite graph, this is the convex hull of incidence vectors of matchings.The additional equalities
$$p_v=1\qquad(v\in P_0)$$
restrict  $x$  to a face. If
$$x=\sum_i\lambda_i\mathbf1_{M_i},
\qquad
\lambda_i>0,\quad \sum_i\lambda_i=1,$$
then for each old endpoint  $v$ ,
$$1=p_v(x)=\sum_i\lambda_i p_v(\mathbf1_{M_i}).$$
Every term on the right is either  $0$  or  $1$ , so every positive-weight matching  $M_i$  covers  $v$ . This holds simultaneously for all old endpoints.That statement concerns the matching marginal  $x$ . It does not construct compatible selections for the individual matchings.If the joint fractional system is written schematically as
$$\mathcal F
=
\{(t,x):x\in P_G,\ At+Bx\le b,\ p_v(x)=1\ (v\in P_0)\},$$
integrality of  $P_G$  does not imply
$$\mathcal F
=
\operatorname{conv}\{\text{feasible integral selection/matching pairs}\}.$$
The missing implication would require, for the particular pair  $(t,x)$ , compatible selections for matching summands whose average is  $t$ . A convex decomposition of  $x$  alone supplies no such compatibility.Accordingly, once full feasibility of the displayed witness is established:It disproves  $J\le18m+29$  as an implication over the specified real relaxation.Every inequality valid for the matching polytope is already satisfied by its  $x$ -coordinate.Even matching-only inequalities valid specifically for matchings covering all old endpoints cannot remove it.No valid linear-combination certificate from those constraints can prove the violated bound.Indeed, the conclusion is logically stronger than the linear-combination statement: a feasible counterexample rules out any sound deduction of that bound over the same real feasible set.The note appropriately leaves open stronger joint occupation inequalities, integrality arguments, selection/matching disjunctions, and freezing conditions. Nothing in the construction establishes that the actual integer frontier fails.6.
